content:
We need to find a retrosynthetic template for carbonyl-ene reaction. The forward reaction: carbonyl + alkene -> new C-C bond, forming hydroxyl and five-membered ring. So the retrosynthesis would break a C-C bond (forming a carbonyl and an alkene). The target molecule has a cyclopentanol fused? Let's examine SMILES: [CH2:1]=[C:2]([c:3]1[cH:4][cH:5][cH:6][cH:7][cH:8]1)[C@@H:9]1[CH2:10][CH2:11][CH2:12][C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18]

Interpretation: There's an exocyclic alkene attached to a phenyl ring (c1ccccc1). The alkene carbon (C2) attached to phenyl and to C1 (CH2). That carbon also attached to C9 which is part of a cyclopentane ring (C9-10-11-12-13). C13 has OH and attached to CF3 (C15 with three Fs). So the cyclopentane ring has a hydroxyl at C13 and a CF3 substituent at C15? Actually C15 is attached to C13? Wait: [C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18] means C13 is attached to OH and to C15 which is CF3 group (C with three Fs). So the cyclopentane ring includes C13 bearing OH and attached to CF3 carbon.

The carbonyl-ene reaction likely formed the cyclopentanol from a carbonyl (maybe a ketone) and an alkene (the exocyclic alkene). So retrosynthetic step: break the C-C bond between C9 (the carbon attached to alkene) and C13? Actually the new C-C bond formed in forward is between the alkene carbon (C2) and the allylic carbon (C9?) Wait carbonyl-ene: carbonyl (C=O) reacts with alkene; the allylic hydrogen transfers to carbonyl oxygen forming OH, and new C-C bond forms between carbonyl carbon and alkene carbon. So in product we have a new C-C bond between carbonyl carbon (now becomes OH-bearing carbon) and alkene carbon. In our product, the OH is on C13 (part of cyclopentane). The alkene carbon is C2 (exocyclic). So likely the carbonyl carbon originally was C13 (now bearing OH). The alkene carbon is C2. So the bond between C2 and C13 is formed in forward. In product we have that bond already? Yes C2 is attached to C9? Wait C2 attached to C9? The SMILES: [CH2:1]=[C:2]([c:3]1... ) [C@@H:9]1... So C2 attached to C9 (the chiral carbon of cyclopentane). So the bond is between C2 and C9, not C13. Actually C9 is the carbon bearing the ring; C13 is another carbon in ring with OH. The carbonyl carbon would be C13? But the new bond is between carbonyl carbon and alkene carbon; that would be C13 to C2. But SMILES shows C2 attached to C9, not C13. Let's map: The cyclopentane ring: C9 (chiral) - CH2-10 - CH2-11 - CH2-12 - C13 (chiral) - back to C9? Actually [C@@H:9]1[CH2:10][CH2:11][CH2:12][C@@:13]1... So ring: C9-10-11-12-13 back to C9. So C9 is attached to C2 (exocyclic alkene). C13 has OH and CF3. So the new bond formed is between C2 and C9 (makes sense). The carbonyl carbon originally was C9? But C9 is not carbonyl; after reaction, carbonyl becomes OH at C13? Wait carbonyl-ene: carbonyl carbon becomes attached to alkene carbon, and carbonyl oxygen becomes OH after hydrogen shift. The OH ends up on carbonyl oxygen (now alcohol). In product, OH is on C13, not on C9. So maybe carbonyl carbon was C13, and after reaction, the new bond formed between C13 and C2, and OH is on C13. But SMILES shows C13 not attached to C2. So maybe the SMILES representation is different: The bond between C2 and C9 is the new bond, and OH is on C13 (different). That suggests a different reaction: maybe a cyclization via intramolecular carbonyl-ene where carbonyl is on C13, alkene is internal, forming a new C-C bond between C13 and C2, and the allylic hydrogen from C9 transfers to carbonyl oxygen, giving OH on C13 and forming a double bond shift? But the product shows C9 attached to C2, not C13. So maybe the forward reaction is a carbonyl-ene that forms a five-membered ring (the cyclopentane) from a linear precursor containing a carbonyl and an alkene. In retrosynthesis, we need to break the C-C bond between C2 and C9, generating a carbonyl at C13? Hmm.

Better approach: Use tool to search templates with functional groups broken: ketones, C-C double bonds; formed: aliphatic hydroxyl, five-membered rings. Let's get available functional groups to correct naming.
